newsitem.title: UK: LIFFE cocoa retraces after hitting one-year high.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE cocoa retraces after hitting one-year high.

text.p: LIFFE cocoa futures retraced to finish broadly lower on Friday after an early breakthrough to new one-year high faltered on pre-weekend selling, traders said.
They said specs and trade selling accelerated amid perceptions that the two-week rally showed no further upside potential.
"Jobbers liquidated their longs and people were squaring off since after two weeks there are no further progress," said one trader.
Benchmark September broke the immediate 1,140 stg a tonne barrier to hit the one-year high of 1,141 stg.
But it stepped back, lost a struggle to defend the critical chart support at 1,130 mark, and came down further to end 19 lower at 1,111.
Cocoa started the day on an encouraging note, helped by carry-over buying from Thursday.
But the upward momentum faded as New York, unable to maintain its overnight strength, came in lower on profit-taking.
Traders said cocoa was also vulnerable to a sell-off ahead of the U.S. CFTC Commitment of Traders rreport, due later tonight, which could show a sharp increase in speculative long positions.
Cocoa's rally since last week was mainly chart-driven but some traders said bulls were also encouraged by a promising longer-term fundamental picture
Cocoa pod counters are not due to return from West Africa until the beginning of July but very preliminary forecasts point to a less favourable supply prospects in Ivory Coast.
But others said with the current "silly season" in cocoa, they could expect a lot of crop rumours.

Early 1997/98 Ivory Coast crop estimates vary from a 785,000 tonnes-mark (main crop) by U.S.-based crop analyst Hans Kilian, according to traders, to a more optimistic 1.1 million tonnes for the whole of 1997/98 by Swiss chocolate giant Callebaut Barry, which has two factories in Ivory Coast.

In other news, British trader ED&F Man Group Plc said on Friday it signed a definitive deal to sell its cocoa processing business to U.S. group Archer Daniels Midland Co for $108 million in cash plus the assumption of debt.

The move involve selling its entire six processing units -- two in the United States, one in UK, one in Canada, one in Brazil and one in Poland. The units have a combined capacity of 160,000 tonnes a year.
But Man would retain its profitable cocoa sourcing operations and its international cocoa merchanting business. -- Jalil Hamid, London newsroom +44 171 542 4985
